title: Quantum Simulation of Si/SiGe Devices with Experimentally Calibrated Micromagnet Effects
authors: Andrii Sokolov, Conor Power, Mathieu Moras, Claude Rohrbacher, Brian Malone, Sergey Amitonov, Agostino Apra, Amir Sammak, Nodar Samkharadze, Elena Blokhina
abstract: Silicon-based spin qubits in Si/SiGe heterostructures are a leading platform for scalable quantum computing, yet bridging the gap between theoretical computer-aided design(CAD) models and experimental reality remains a significant challenge. Standard simulations often fail to capture critical physical phenomena, such as interface dipoles, parasitic charge accumulation, and the magnetic hysteresis of on-chip micromagnets. In this work, we present a comprehensive, experimentally calibrated 3D simulation pipeline for a 6-dot Si/SiGe device. We refine the semiconductor band alignment and introduce a semi-empirical classical charge screening model to accurately capture the formation of parasitic wells and their suppression of gate lever-arms. Furthermore, we apply the Jiles-Atherton model to account for the hysteresis and pre-magnetization of integrated cobalt micromagnets, successfully reproducing the experimental resonant frequencies across all six qubits. By coupling these calibrated electrostatic and magnetic profiles into a time-dependent rotating wave approximation (RWA) Hamiltonian, we reproduce experimental observables, including microwave power chevrons. This framework provides a robust foundation for predicting device behavior, evaluating microwave line losses, and optimizing future scalable spin qubit architectures prior to fabrication.
summary: This paper presents an advanced, fully calibrated simulation framework for spin qubits in Si/SiGe devices, designed to overcome discrepancies between theory and experiment. By integrating complex physics—including charge screening effects and magnetic hysteresis via the Jiles-Atherton model—the authors successfully predict key experimental signatures like resonant frequencies and power chevrons. This robust tool significantly advances the predictive capability for scalable quantum computing architectures.
main_problem: The primary challenge is bridging the gap between theoretical quantum device simulations and actual experimental measurements for silicon-based spin qubits.
main_result: The authors developed a comprehensive, experimentally calibrated simulation pipeline that successfully reproduces key experimental observables, such as resonant frequencies and microwave power chevrons, across a multi-dot qubit array.
method: The work combines advanced 3D classical electrostatics (Poisson solver) with micromagnetism (Jiles-Atherton model) and quantum dynamics (time-dependent RWA Hamiltonian) to model the coupled system.
model_or_system: The system is a Si/SiGe heterostructure containing a 6-dot quantum dot array, coupled to integrated cobalt micromagnets. The simulation incorporates refined band alignment, a semi-empirical charge screening model, and the Jiles-Atherton model for magnetic hysteresis.
key_observables: Microwave power chevrons, qubit resonant frequencies ($f = g\mu_B / h B$), and gate lever-arm variation ($dE_C/dV_{	ext{gate}}$).
important_parameters: Microwave frequency ($\omega_0$), external magnetic field ($B_{	ext{ext}}$), and material parameters calibrated against experimental data.
main_assumptions: The model assumes the use of the Rotating-Wave Approximation (RWA) for dynamics and required significant empirical calibration for charge screening and magnetic hysteresis.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the FEM model components, band alignment shifts, the calibration of Jiles-Atherton parameters, and direct comparisons between simulated and measured power chevrons for the six qubits.
paper_structure: The paper systematically addresses simulation failures by first refining the electrostatic model (charge screening) and then incorporating the magnetic hysteresis via the Jiles-Atherton model, finally coupling these results into a time-dependent RWA Hamiltonian to predict dynamic observables.
why_interesting: The rigorous coupling of classical charge effects (electrostatics) and magnetic dynamics (micromagnetics) into a quantum Hamiltonian provides a highly realistic framework for modeling solid-state qubits, which is crucial for understanding decoherence and control.
